steps.x: The scapula and humerus form the glenohumeral joint. The glenoid cavity is shallow: stability depends largely on the rotator cuff muscles.
It arises from the supraspinous fossa, passes under the acromion and inserts on the superior facet of the greater tubercle. It initiates abduction and is the most frequently injured tendon.
They occupy the posterior surface of the scapula and insert on the middle and inferior facets of the greater tubercle. They are the external rotators of the shoulder.
It occupies the subscapular fossa, on the anterior surface of the scapula, and inserts on the lesser tubercle. It is the main internal rotator.
The glenohumeral capsule is reinforced by the glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments. The coracoacromial ligament forms the roof of the subacromial space, where the supraspinatus is impinged.

The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; the axillary nerve supplies teres minor and the deltoid. An axillary nerve injury after dislocation leaves anesthesia over the lateral aspect of the arm.

q.p: Which rotator cuff muscle is the main internal rotator of the shoulder?

steps.x: The carpal bones form a channel concave toward the palmar side. Its borders are the scaphoid and trapezium laterally, and the pisiform and hamate medially.
The flexor retinaculum closes the channel and turns it into an inextensible osteofibrous tunnel. Any increase in volume within it compresses its contents.

steps.t: The tendons that pass through it
steps.x: Four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus pass through, surrounded by synovial sheaths.
show: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

steps.x: It is the most superficial structure in the tunnel and the one that is compressed. It gives off the palmar digital nerves for the thumb, index, middle and the lateral half of the ring finger.
show: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve

steps.x: The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. Their atrophy indicates advanced compression.
show: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis

q.p: Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?

steps.x: The femur articulates with the tibia and the patella. The fibula does not take part in the knee joint, but serves as an anchor for the fibular collateral ligament.
The anterior cruciate prevents the tibia from sliding forward; the posterior, backward. They are examined with the Lachman and drawer tests.
The tibial collateral resists valgus and is attached to the medial meniscus; the fibular collateral resists varus and is extracapsular.
show: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

steps.x: C-shaped fibrocartilages that distribute load. The medial one, less mobile because of its attachment to the tibial collateral, is injured more often.
The patellar ligament joins the patella to the tibial tuberosity, and the retinacula stabilize it at the sides.

q.p: Which structure prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur?

steps.x: The tibiofibular mortise embraces the talus. The lateral malleolus descends lower than the medial one, which favors inversion sprains.
It runs from the lateral malleolus to the neck of the talus and is tensed in plantar flexion and inversion. It is the first and most frequently injured.
The calcaneofibular ligament is injured in moderate sprains; the posterior talofibular, the strongest, only in severe ones.
The tibiofibular ligaments join the tibia and fibula. Their injury, the high ankle sprain, takes longer to heal.
The fibularis longus and brevis evert the foot and protect against inversion; their tendons pass under the fibular retinacula.

q.p: Which is the most frequently injured ligament in a lateral ankle sprain?

steps.x: The anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the roots of the plexus, which emerge between the anterior and middle scalenes.
C5 and C6 form the upper trunk, C7 the middle and C8–T1 the lower. Erb palsy affects the upper trunk.
Each trunk divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The posterior divisions form the posterior cord, origin of the axillary and radial nerves.
show: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus

steps.x: The musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, axillary and radial nerves supply the entire upper limb.
The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior: its injury produces a winged scapula. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

q.p: Which nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?

steps.x: The inguinal ligament forms the base; the sartorius, the lateral border, and adductor longus, the medial border.
The iliopsoas laterally and the pectineus medially form the floor of the triangle.
From lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery and femoral vein. The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point and the vein lies just medial to it.
It ascends along the medial aspect of the thigh and drains into the femoral vein through the saphenous opening. It is used as a graft in coronary surgery.

q.p: What is the order from lateral to medial in the femoral triangle?

steps.x: Five large-bodied vertebrae bear the greatest axial load and form the lumbar lordosis over the sacrum.
The nucleus pulposus, surrounded by the annulus fibrosus, distributes the load. L4–L5 and L5–S1 account for most herniations.

The anterior longitudinal ligament limits extension; the posterior, weaker at the lumbar level, explains why herniations are posterolateral. The ligamenta flava, interspinous and supraspinous ligaments limit flexion.
It arises from L4 to S3 and descends through the gluteal region and the posterior thigh. Compression of its roots by a herniation produces sciatica.

q.p: At which levels do most lumbar disc herniations occur?

steps.x: Rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius converge in the quadriceps tendon. Only rectus femoris also crosses the hip.
The patella, a sesamoid bone, increases the lever arm of the quadriceps. The patellar ligament transmits the force to the tibial tuberosity.
The femoral nerve (L2–L4) supplies the entire quadriceps. The patellar reflex tests L3–L4.

q.p: Which head of the quadriceps crosses two joints?

steps.x: The two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx form a ring closed anteriorly at the pubic symphysis. In women the pelvis is wider and lower, the pelvic inlet is oval, the ischial spines are farther apart and the pubic arch exceeds 80°: all of this widens the birth canal.

They join the sacrum to the ischial spine (sacrospinous) and to the ischial tuberosity (sacrotuberous). They convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, through which the pudendal vessels and nerve pass toward the perineum.

The obturator internus lines the lateral wall and its thickened fascia forms the tendinous arch of the levator ani, a band from the pubis to the ischial spine where the pelvic floor is anchored. The piriformis closes the posterior wall.

The levator ani (pubococcygeus, puboanal/puborectalis and iliococcygeus) and the coccygeus form a funnel-shaped hammock that supports the viscera. In the midline it leaves the urogenital hiatus, through which the urethra and vagina pass. The puborectalis sling pulls the rectum forward and forms the anorectal angle, key to continence.

From front to back: bladder, uterus with the vagina, and rectum. The uterus is usually in anteversion (tilted forward over the bladder) and anteflexion. Between the uterus and rectum lies the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity.

The uterus is suspended by the cardinal (Mackenrodt) and uterosacral ligaments, which fix the cervix to the pelvic walls; the round ligament keeps it in anteversion and the broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that carries the vessels. Their weakening, together with that of the levator ani, produces prolapse.

Below the pelvic diaphragm, the superficial perineal space contains the crura of the clitoris with the ischiocavernosus, the vestibular bulbs with the bulbospongiosus, the Bartholin glands and the superficial transverse perineal muscle. All converge on the perineal body, together with the external anal sphincter.

The uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac, crosses over the ureter ("water under the bridge"), a critical detail in hysterectomy. The pudendal nerve and vessels leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and enter the perineum through the lesser one, wrapping around the ischial spine: this is where the pudendal block is performed in obstetrics.

q.p: Which muscle forms the anorectal angle and is key to fecal continence?
Which structure does the uterine artery cross above, next to the cervix?
What is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in women?
At which bony landmark is the pudendal nerve block performed?
Which ligaments mainly support the cervix, and their injury favors prolapse?

steps.x: The heart occupies the middle mediastinum, with two thirds to the left of the midline and the apex pointing down, forward and to the left. It receives the venae cavae in the right atrium and the four pulmonary veins in the left; the pulmonary trunk and the ascending aorta leave the ventricles.

They arise from the aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve. The right coronary runs in the right atrioventricular groove; the left divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, which supplies the anterior part of the septum, and the circumflex. Venous blood returns through the coronary sinus to the right atrium.

A frontal section opens the four cavities. The walls of the left ventricle are about three times thicker than those of the right, because they propel blood into the systemic circulation at higher pressure. The interventricular septum separates the two ventricles.

The tricuspid (right, three leaflets) and mitral (left, two leaflets: anterior and posterior) open in diastole to fill the ventricles and close in systole: their closure produces the first heart sound. The leaflets are held by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles, which contract to prevent them from prolapsing into the atria.

Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve
Inferior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal papillary muscle of right ventricle
Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle
Anterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve
Anterior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Anterior papillary muscle of left ventricle

steps.x: The pulmonary and aortic valves each have three semilunar cusps. They close at the end of systole and produce the second sound. The coronary arteries arise behind the right and left coronary cusps of the aorta; the third is the non-coronary cusp.
show: Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve

steps.x: Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta. Activate the vein and artery layer to follow it on the model.
show: Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve

Anterior papillary muscle of left ventricle

q.p: Which structures hold the leaflets of the atrioventricular valves?
o: The chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles
The fibrous ring of the pulmonary valve

q.p: What produces the first heart sound?
o: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves

q.p: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
o: From the aortic sinuses, above the aortic valve

q.p: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker?
o: Because it pumps into the systemic circulation, at higher pressure
Because it receives a larger volume of blood
Because it contains the mitral valve
Because it is closer to the pericardium

t: The brain from the inside: nuclei and ventricles

steps.x: The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata) joins the brain to the spinal cord and contains the cranial nerve nuclei and vital centers. The cerebellum, behind it, coordinates movement; its tonsils can herniate through the foramen magnum when intracranial pressure rises.

The lateral ventricles, one in each hemisphere, communicate through the interventricular foramina with the third ventricle, between the two thalami; this continues through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, in front of the cerebellum. The choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid (about 500 ml a day). Its obstruction causes hydrocephalus.

The caudate nucleus surrounds the lateral ventricle; the putamen and globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus. Together with the substantia nigra and the subthalamus they control the initiation and scaling of movement: their degeneration produces Parkinson disease (substantia nigra) and Huntington disease (caudate).

In a coronal section the following can be recognized, from medial to lateral: third ventricle, thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus and putamen), external capsule, claustrum and insula. Above, the corpus callosum crosses the midline and forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
show: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci)

steps.x: The hippocampus, in the wall of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, consolidates memory; the fornix carries its fibers to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus. The amygdala, in front of the hippocampus, processes fear and emotions. Its involvement explains the recent memory loss of Alzheimer disease.

An axial section, such as that of a CT or MRI of the skull, shows in a single plane the frontal horns of the ventricles, the head of the caudate, the lentiform nucleus, the internal capsule shaped like a V open outward, and the thalamus. Try the CT and MRI modes in the Planes tab.

q.p: Which structure connects the third and fourth ventricles?
Which two nuclei form the lentiform nucleus?
Where is most of the cerebrospinal fluid produced?
Which structure is essential for forming new memories?

steps.t: The sensory nerves: I, II and VIII
steps.x: The olfactory nerve (I) crosses the cribriform plate of the ethmoid; the optic nerve (II) leaves the orbit through the optic canal toward the chiasm; the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) enters the internal acoustic meatus beside the facial nerve. They are purely sensory nerves.

steps.t: The motors of the eye: III, IV and VI
steps.x: The oculomotor nerve (III) supplies almost all the extraocular muscles, the levator palpebrae and, with parasympathetic fibers, the pupil; the trochlear nerve (IV), the superior oblique; the abducens nerve (VI), the lateral rectus. A lesion of III leaves the eye "down and out" with ptosis and mydriasis.
The largest of the cranial nerves: its three branches (ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular) collect sensation from the face, and the mandibular branch supplies the muscles of mastication.

It leaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle, runs through the facial canal of the temporal bone and exits through the stylomastoid foramen to supply the muscles of facial expression. Its peripheral lesion (Bell palsy) paralyzes the whole hemiface.

Glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) exit through the jugular foramen: swallowing, taste from the posterior third of the tongue and the parasympathetic innervation of the thorax and abdomen. The accessory nerve (XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; the hypoglossal nerve (XII), the tongue: if injured, the tongue deviates toward the injured side.

q.p: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye?
An eye deviated down and out with ptosis and a dilated pupil suggests a lesion of the…
Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of mastication?

steps.x: It divides the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle. It turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side. It is supplied by the accessory nerve (XI).
The sternohyoid and omohyoid lower the hyoid in swallowing and phonation; the mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth.
It wraps around the trachea below the cricoid cartilage; its isthmus crosses the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings. It moves with swallowing because it is attached to the larynx.

It contains the common carotid artery (which divides at the level of the thyroid cartilage into internal and external), the internal jugular vein laterally and the vagus nerve posteriorly. The carotid pulse is palpated at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid.

q.p: Where does the common carotid usually divide?
o: At the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage
At the level of the angle of the mandible
At the level of the cricoid

q.p: Which structure lies inside the carotid sheath, behind the vessels?

steps.x: The external intercostals raise the ribs in inspiration (like a bucket handle); the internal ones help in forced expiration. Along the inferior border of each rib runs the intercostal neurovascular bundle: that is why punctures are made along the superior border of the lower rib.
The main inspiratory muscle: on contracting it descends and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax. It is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5): "C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive."

The right has three lobes (upper, middle and lower) and the left two, with the lingula in place of the middle lobe. Each lobe is divided into bronchopulmonary segments, surgical units with their own bronchus and artery.
The trachea divides at the level of T4–T5 (carina). The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical: that is why aspirated foreign bodies usually go to the right lung.
Between both lungs: heart and great vessels, trachea, esophagus, vagus and phrenic nerves, thoracic duct and the azygos vein, which drains into the superior vena cava.

q.p: Why do aspirated foreign bodies tend to go to the right lung?
o: Its main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical
Because of the position of the heart on the right
Because the left bronchus has no cartilage

q.p: Which roots form the phrenic nerve?
Along which border of the rib is thoracentesis performed?
o: Along the superior border of the lower rib
Along the inferior border of the upper rib
Through the middle of the space

steps.x: The liver occupies the right hypochondrium under the diaphragm; the gallbladder, on its inferior surface, projects its fundus at the crossing of the costal margin with the rectus abdominis (Murphy point). The stomach, in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium, continues into the duodenum.

The head of the pancreas lies in the duodenal C-loop; the body crosses in front of the aorta and the vena cava, and the tail reaches the spleen. The common bile duct and the pancreatic duct open together at the ampulla of Vater, in the 2nd part of the duodenum.

Jejunum and ileum occupy the center of the abdomen; the colon frames it: ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid, which continues into the rectum. The colon has taeniae coli, haustra and epiploic appendages, which distinguish it from the small intestine.
Retroperitoneal, at the level of T12–L3; the right one somewhat lower because of the liver. The adrenal gland rests on its upper pole.

steps.t: Blood supply of the digestive tract
steps.x: The abdominal aorta gives off the celiac trunk (foregut: stomach, liver, spleen), the superior mesenteric artery (midgut: from the duodenum to the transverse colon) and the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut: down to the rectum). Venous blood returns to the liver through the portal vein.

q.p: Which artery supplies from the duodenum to the transverse colon?
Where do the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct open?
o: In the 2nd part of the duodenum (ampulla of Vater)
In the 4th part of the duodenum

steps.x: From superficial to deep: external oblique (fibers running downward and forward, "hands in the pockets"), internal oblique (fibers perpendicular to those of the external) and transversus abdominis (horizontal fibers, the "corset"). Their aponeuroses form the rectus sheath.

It runs from the 5th–7th costal cartilages and the xiphoid process to the pubis. Its tendinous intersections divide it into bellies and adhere to the anterior layer of its sheath. It flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.

A midline raphe formed by the interlacing of the aponeuroses of the three broad muscles, from the xiphoid process to the pubis, with the umbilical ring at its midpoint. Its widening is rectus diastasis; the midline laparotomy is made through it.

Above the arcuate line (about 4 cm below the umbilicus) the aponeurosis of the internal oblique splits: the anterior layer passes in front of the rectus and the posterior layer behind it. Below it, all the aponeuroses pass in front and the rectus rests only on the transversalis fascia.

The inguinal ligament is the thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. Above it runs the inguinal canal, with the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves and the inferior epigastric vessels in its posterior wall.

q.p: Which abdominal wall muscle has fibers directed downward and forward?
Which structure forms the thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis?
Below the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis rests posteriorly on…
o: The posterior layer of the sheath
The parietal peritoneum directly, without fascia

steps.x: The bulkiest muscle in the body: it extends and laterally rotates the hip and inserts on the gluteal tuberosity and the iliotibial tract. It is key for rising from a chair and climbing stairs.
Abductors and stabilizers of the pelvis in single-leg stance. Their weakness produces the Trendelenburg sign. They are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Piriformis, gemelli, obturator internus, quadratus femoris and obturator externus. The piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into a suprapiriform space (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) and an infrapiriform space (sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal and pudendal).

The thickest nerve in the body (L4–S3): it exits below the piriformis, descends between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity and divides, usually at the apex of the popliteal fossa, into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Injections are given in the superolateral quadrant of the buttock to avoid injuring it.

q.p: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus?
Where does the sciatic nerve usually leave the pelvis?
In which quadrant of the buttock are intramuscular injections given?

steps.x: A diamond behind the knee: above, the biceps femoris (lateral) and the semimembranosus and semitendinosus (medial); below, the two heads of the gastrocnemius.
From superficial to deep: tibial and common fibular nerves, popliteal vein and, deepest and next to the bone, the popliteal artery. Its pulse is palpated with the knee flexed.
The popliteus unlocks the knee at the start of flexion by rotating the tibia medially. Above it lie the capsule and the oblique popliteal ligament.

q.p: What is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa?
Which muscle "unlocks" the knee at the start of flexion?

steps.x: From the medial epicondyle: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris. Its tendinopathy is medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow).
show: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

steps.x: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints; its tendons pass through the carpal tunnel.
show: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

steps.x: Flexor digitorum profundus (distal interphalangeal joints), flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus. The lateral half of the flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the median nerve (anterior interosseous) and the medial half by the ulnar nerve.
The median nerve passes between the heads of pronator teres and under flexor digitorum superficialis; the ulnar nerve, behind the medial epicondyle and under flexor carpi ulnaris.
show: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

q.p: Which muscle flexes the distal interphalangeal joint of the fingers?
Between which structures does the median nerve pass at the elbow?
o: Between the heads of pronator teres

steps.x: Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis: they allow opposition. They are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, except the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.
show: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis

steps.x: With its oblique and transverse heads it brings the thumb toward the palm (key pinch). It is supplied by the ulnar nerve: its weakness gives Froment sign.
Abductor, flexor brevis and opponens of the little finger, supplied by the ulnar nerve.
show: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

steps.x: The lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus; with the interossei they flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. The palmar interossei adduct the fingers and the dorsal ones abduct them ("PAD and DAB").

q.p: Which nerve supplies adductor pollicis?
Which muscles abduct the fingers of the hand?

steps.x: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms and the first three metatarsals; the lateral arch, by the calcaneus, cuboid and 4th–5th metatarsals.

The plantar aponeurosis joins the calcaneus to the toes and tenses the arch in the late stance phase (windlass mechanism). Beneath it lie abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.
Quadratus plantae and lumbricals; then flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis and the interossei.

The long plantar ligament and the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament ("spring ligament") support the arch, together with the tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus, which cross the sole like a stirrup.

q.p: Which structure tenses the arch at toe-off (windlass mechanism)?
Which tendons form the "stirrup" of the foot?
o: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus

steps.x: Anterior: pectoralis major and minor. Posterior: subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi. Medial: serratus anterior over the chest wall. Lateral: intertubercular groove of the humerus.
show: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

steps.x: The axillary artery continues the subclavian from the border of the 1st rib and pectoralis minor divides it into three parts. The axillary vein lies medial.
Its cords surround the 2nd part of the axillary artery and give the terminal nerves of the upper limb: musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, axillary and radial.
Pectoral (anterior), central, lateral, subscapular (posterior) and apical; they drain the upper limb and most of the breast.

q.p: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
To which group of nodes does most of the lymph from the breast drain first?
